Some handy references on Newcomb-Benford-Law basics:

  • http://datagenetics.com/blog/march52012/index.html
  • https://www.statisticshowto.datasciencecentral.com/benfords-law/
  • http://www.statisticalconsultants.co.nz/blog/benfords-law-and-accounting-fraud-detection-m.html
  • http://mathworld.wolfram.com/BenfordsLaw.html
  • https://ibmathsresources.com/2017/04/01/bedfords-law-to-catch-fraudsters/
  • https://www.r-bloggers.com/benfords-law/
  • https://m.doc88.com/p-9935177204203.html (advanced) etc...

For this challenge there are only two parts this time.

  1. read a list of numbers and display a summary of leading digit frequency or occurrence.
  2. generate a list of numbers that hopefully tend towards Benford's Law distributions.

Advanced math is not requred for basic programming, even if going deeper than we do here would lead to advanced math. This is meant to be [Easy].

Notes:

  • Some of the references have a formula using base-10 logorithms, a Benford's Law of hexadecimal values would probably use base-16 logorithms but that would be another problem...
  • Typical random number generators generally have "uniform distribution". Benford's Law can be generated with a "log-uniform distribution", meaning that an exponent is evenly distributed to a power function.
  • Some programming languages or statistical/scientific libraries provide random number generators with different distributions, but you may have to impliment loguniform on top of basic random as such.
int loguniform(int MIN, int MAX) {
 float lo = log(MIN), hi = log(MAX);
 float t = between(lo, hi);
 return round( exp(t) );
}
/* or some variation... */
  • It is something of a mystery why Benford's Law occurrs in observed phenomena. There are advanced mathematics on this topic, but we will regard log-uniform distribution to be "good enough".
  • You are, of course, free to do something more advanced or just different as long as good results.
  • You are not required to do advanced test of statical significance or chi-tests or any such thing, not for an [Easy] challenge. If you would like to report a pass/fail on whether a data set conforms to Benford's Law then having all probabilities within 5% of expected for a set of 5000+ items is "good enough".
  • Many natural phenomena follow a Power Law or Pareto Distribution but we provide no explaination why this happens. A Power Law distribution is one way of produce Benford's Law results, making it the Easiest Thing That Could Work™.
  • Benford's Law looks at the leading digit (or sometimes a certain place to the right of leading digit). You can't simply take a number modulo 10 because that would be the last digit instead of first. A convenient way to get leading digit might be to write to a string and peek at first character. Dividing a number by 10 until lesser than 10 would also work.
  • You may need to truncate a floating point number to an integer or handle numbers in some way, either for digits or random function or some other step. Printing numbers to a string may bypass some issues. We don't consider decimals starting with a zero so this note may be moot.
  • Benford's Law is used on observed data in some dimension (e.g. feet, inches, meters, grams, seconds etc.) but tends to work no matter what dimension. You can convert distance measures in feet to meters and the data should generally still follow Benford's Law. This property is known as "dimensional independence".
  • Benford's Law does not generally work on data that has artificial origins or comes from a source that isn't distributed like normal data. That is what makes Part 2 a challenge. For example, if you try using word length of the words from the enable1.txt word list you get terrible results. If you use numbers from a basic random number generator it would probably be roughly uniform and not look like Benford data either.
  • OT but interesting: Mandarin Chinese has different units or "Measure Words" for use with numbers of objects in a linguistic class. For example "3 books" in Mandarin would be 3 with the appropriate suffix for the class of object book after it. In a way use of numbers in Mandarin often has a dimension to it! Most languages (including Mandarin) have both Cardinal Numbers and Ordinal Numbers. Some languages like to use certain words like the equivalent of "pair" when referring to certain objects (e.g. "a pair of shoes" for two shoes). But Mandarin has Measure Words as a sort of linguistic dimension.

Have fun analyzing data and generating simulated data!
